title: Embedding elastic reservoir and priority dequeue for smoother throughput
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Background: Customers with bursty embedding workloads experience high p99 latency and frequent token-cost spikes when traffic suddenly increases. Current autoscaler reacts too slowly to microbursts and the single FIFO ingress queue causes head-of-line blocking from a few large tenants. Proposal: Implement an "elastic reservoir" — a short-lived burst buffer pooled across embedding workers that can absorb microbursts — combined with a priority-aware dequeue that separates short/fast requests (low cost, low seq len) from heavy batch requests. The system should maintain per-tenant fairness, configurable burst budgets, and integrate with existing rate-limit hooks and the Dedicated capacity planner.
design_notes: Introduce a small in-memory reservoir on each ingress node with tokenized capacity units representing amortized embedding cost.
Requests first try reservoir admission; admitted requests get fast-path routing to a hot worker pool (cold-start avoidance via KV cache warmup hints).
Priority classes: realtime (short seq, low tokens), standard, bulk. Realtime gets preemptive admission during short bursts but is rate-limited by a reservoir budget per-tenant and global headroom.
When reservoir is exhausted, requests fall back to normal queueing with graceful 429 hints and ETA headers for client backoff guidance.
Autoscaler integration: reservoir occupancy feeds a microburst signal to the autoscaler so it can speculatively spin up hot workers before queue growth becomes visible at the p99.
Expose controls in Console: per-tenant burst budget, global reservoir size, realtime token threshold, and observed hit-rate metrics.
Security & fairness: enforce max burst-per-tenant and a decay model to prevent noisy-neighbor exhaustion.
Compatibility: keep existing embedding API unchanged. Add optional response headers X-Reservoir-Admitted and X-Estimated-Queue-ETA.
Fallbacks: when Dedicated pools are at capacity, reservoir admission should prefer same-tenant warm workers or degrade to a best-effort delayed enqueue rather than failing outright.
acceptance_criteria: p99 embedding latency for mixed workload (50% realtime, 30% standard, 20% bulk) reduced by >=25% during 60s bursts in internal canary compared to baseline
Reservoir admission rate and per-tenant burst caps observable in Console with to-the-second telemetry
No regression in end-to-end throughput for steady-state traffic (within ±5%)
Autoscaler receives microburst signal and launches additional hot workers within 30s in test harness
Headers X-Reservoir-Admitted and X-Estimated-Queue-ETA returned for admitted/queued requests and validated by SDK integration tests
Security review completed and noisy-neighbor abuse mitigations documented
implementation_plan: Spike (2d): prototype per-node in-memory reservoir + admission logic in embedding ingress service; synthetic load test harness to simulate mixed tenants
Design review (1d): present design with SRE and Security; collect feedback on limits and metrics
Core implementation (7d): reservoir bookkeeping, priority dequeue paths, integration with existing queueing and rate-limiter middleware
Autoscaler hook (3d): emit occupancy and admission-rate metrics; implement microburst signal consumer in autoscaler
Console telemetry (2d): add dashboard panels and expose controls for reservoir sizes and per-tenant budgets
Canary rollout (5d): start with internal customers and low global reservoir sizing; monitor SLOs and adjust
Gradual ramp (2w): increase reservoir capacity and enable for select customer cohorts; watch thermal metrics and cost signals
Postmortem & tuning (ongoing): collect results, tune decay model and default budgets
testing_plan: Unit tests covering admission, budget accounting, and decay behavior
Load tests with multi-tenant burst scenarios in staging: measure p50/p95/p99 under different reservoir sizes
Chaos tests: simulate worker loss and validate reservoir admission falls back to safe enqueue
End-to-end SDK test: verify headers and client-side backoff integration
Cost analysis: run simulations to estimate additional hot-worker minutes and net cost per 1M burst requests
rollout_steps: Feature flag gated: start disabled by default
Internal dogfood cohort with diagnostics enabled
Enable for low-volume customers for 72h and run monitors
If stable, enable for medium-volume customers and continue rolling
Post-rollout configuration: set conservative defaults and add Console tooltips
risks_and_mitigations: Risk: reservoir may enable bursty customers to consume disproportionate hot capacity -> Mitigation: enforce strict per-tenant decay and daily caps
Risk: increased complexity in admission logic could introduce bugs -> Mitigation: feature-flagged rollout, comprehensive unit tests, and staged canary
Risk: hidden cost of speculative hot workers -> Mitigation: telemetry and alerting on cost deltas; conservative autoscaler thresholds
Risk: race conditions between reservoir admission and autoscaler -> Mitigation: idempotent admission tokens and eventual consistency in metrics
